title: Comparison: more than
plainEnglish: It marks the thing you are comparing against, like saying than in English.
whenToUse: Reach for 보다 whenever you rank two things on a scale and want to name the baseline you measure against. It attaches to the standard (B) in the frame A는 B보다 더 + adjective, so the listener hears 'compared to B, A is more …': 동생이 저보다 키가 더 커요 (compared to me, my sibling is taller). Use it for size, speed, price, preference (저는 커피보다 차를 더 좋아해요), and even to soften a choice ('I'd rather'). The intent is always relative ranking, not absolute description, so you grab it the moment an English 'than' would appear.
attachmentRule: Attach 보다 directly to a noun with no spacing change, after both vowels and consonants (사과보다, 물보다). The pattern is A가/는 B보다 더 Adjective.
contrastWith: Sharp contrast: 보다 vs 처럼. 보다 ranks two things and marks the LOSER/baseline (기차가 버스보다 빨라요 = the train beats the bus), while 처럼 means 'like/as' and marks a thing you RESEMBLE, with no winner (기차처럼 빨라요 = fast like a train). Also distinguish 보다 from the verb 보다 'to see' — here it is a particle glued to a noun, not a verb, so 'than' never conjugates.

examples.en: This one is bigger.
examples.note: Simple base: 더 alone already means 'more/bigger'; 보다 is added only when you name what you compare to.

examples.en: My younger sibling is taller than me.
examples.note: Everyday frame A이/가 B보다 …: 보다 sticks to 저 (the baseline), and 키가 크다 'be tall' is the natural collocation for height.

examples.ko: 이 책이 저 책보다 더 재미있어요.
examples.en: This book is more interesting than that book.
examples.note: Two near-identical nouns contrasted: 보다 rides 저 책 (the baseline), so demonstratives 이/저 make the comparison crisp.

examples.ko: 지하철이 버스보다 훨씬 빨라서 지하철로 갈게요.
examples.en: The subway is much faster than the bus, so I'll go by subway.
examples.note: Real situation: 훨씬 'by far' intensifies the gap better than 더 here, and the comparison drives a real decision.

commonMistakes: Sticking 보다 on the subject instead of the baseline: 동생보다 저는 커요 to mean 'I'm taller than my sibling' is backwards — 보다 marks the LOSER, so you need 저는 동생보다 커요. Test: whatever 'than' touches in English is what 보다 touches in Korean.
Saying 더 좋아요 보다 / 좋아해요 보다 as if 보다 follows the adjective like English 'more … than'. 보다 attaches to the NOUN, not the verb: 커피보다 차가 더 좋아요, never 좋아요보다.
studyOrder: Identify the two items A and B you compare
Attach 보다 to the standard B
Add 더 before the adjective for more
Finish with the adjective in 해요 form
beginnerExplanation: 보다 is how Korean says 'than' in a comparison, and the secret is that it attaches to the thing you measure against, not to the subject. Mnemonic: in English 'than' points at the loser ('taller THAN me'), and Korean 보다 hugs that exact same word — so 'than me' is just 저보다. Build it as A는 B보다 더 + adjective: 동생이 저보다 키가 더 커요 means my sibling beats me in height, and 오늘이 어제보다 더 추워요 means today out-colds yesterday. 더 means 'more' and sits right before the adjective; you can drop it and the sentence still compares. Don't confuse this 보다 with the verb 보다 'to see' — here it is a tiny particle stuck to a noun, so it never conjugates. The one trap to avoid is gluing 보다 to the subject; keep it on whatever follows 'than' in English.

title: Optional plural marker
plainEnglish: It marks a noun as plural, but Korean usually leaves it off.
whenToUse: Add 들 only when you deliberately want to spotlight that there are MANY, and it lands most naturally on people: 학생들이 교실에 있어요 (the students are in the classroom), 친구들과 같이 가요 (I go with my friends). Use it when plurality is the point of the sentence or when leaving it off would feel oddly singular for a known group. The intent is emphasis, not grammar — a bare 사과 already covers 'apples', so you switch 들 on for vividness ('all those kids') and switch it off the moment a number, a counter, or plain context already signals quantity.
attachmentRule: Attach 들 to the end of the noun after both vowels and consonants (친구들, 학생들). With a number or counter you normally omit it (사과 세 개, not 사과들 세 개).
contrastWith: Sharp contrast: 들 vs the prefix 매-/the word 모든. 들 just pluralizes (학생들 = students), 모든 means 'every/all' as a determiner before the noun (모든 학생 = every student), and they are not interchangeable — 모든 학생들 is redundant. Versus English -s: -s is obligatory, 들 is optional and emphatic, so a bare noun is usually the unmarked, more natural plural.

examples.en: They're my friends.
examples.note: Simple base: 들 on people reads as a natural group; here it signals more than one friend at a glance.

examples.en: The children are playing in the park.
examples.note: Everyday: 들 spotlights a visible group of kids, and 놀고 있다 'be playing' shows it pairs fine with the progressive.

examples.ko: 오늘 행사에 사람들이 정말 많이 왔어요.
examples.en: A lot of people came to today's event.
examples.note: Here 들 marks a real crowd; paired with 많이 'a lot' it genuinely stresses plurality rather than just decorating the noun.

examples.en: Everyone, please all take your seats.
examples.note: Real situation: 다들 (= 다 + 들) means 'all of you' to a crowd — a fixed, very common spoken use of 들 on a pronoun-like word.

commonMistakes: Copying English and stamping 들 on every plural: 책상들 위에 책들이 많아요 sounds heavy and learner-ish. Drop it where number is obvious — 책상 위에 책이 많아요 is the natural sentence.
Keeping 들 when a counter is present: 사과들 세 개 is wrong because the counter 개 already counts. Say 사과 세 개. The number does the pluralizing, so 들 becomes redundant and is omitted.
studyOrder: Notice Korean nouns do not need a plural mark
Add 들 only to highlight many, usually people
Attach 들 to the end of the noun
Drop 들 when a number or counter appears
beginnerExplanation: 들 turns a noun plural, but the lesson for beginners is that it is optional and Korean usually drops it. Mnemonic: think of 들 as a highlighter, not a rule — you switch it on only when 'there are MANY' is the point. A bare 사과 already covers apple or apples, and context decides, so you don't owe 들 the way English forces -s. You'll see it most with people: 학생들이 교실에 있어요 (the students are in the classroom) or 친구들과 같이 가요 (I go with my friends), and in the set phrase 다들 'everyone'. The big trap is sprinkling 들 onto everything — it sounds clunky, and you must especially leave it off when a counter is present, so it's 사과 세 개 (three apples), never 사과들 세 개. Don't confuse 들 with 모든 'every' either: 모든 학생 already means every student, so adding 들 is overkill.

title: Counting with counters
plainEnglish: To count things you use a native number plus a counter word that matches the kind of thing.
whenToUse: Use a counter every time you put a quantity on a concrete thing — objects, people, animals, servings: 사과 두 개 주세요 (two apples, please), 학생 세 명 (three students), 강아지 한 마리 (one puppy), 커피 두 잔 (two coffees). The intent is to count a tangible noun, and Korean refuses a bare number for that, the way English needs 'two SHEETS of paper' or 'two CUPS of coffee' rather than 'two papers'. Pick the counter that matches the category, put it after a NATIVE number, and use this constantly when ordering, shopping, or describing how many of something you see.
attachmentRule: Use NATIVE numbers before counters, and the numbers 1 to 4 change shape: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네 (한 개, 두 명, 세 마리). Order is noun + number + counter (사과 세 개).
contrastWith: Sharp contrast: native vs Sino number systems. Counters take NATIVE numbers (한, 두, 세, 네, 다섯…), so it's 두 개, 세 명. But money, dates, minutes, floors, and phone numbers take SINO numbers (일, 이, 삼, 사…), so it's 이천 원, 삼 월, 십 분. Mixing them — 이 개, 두 월 — is the classic beginner error; match the system to the counter.

examples.en: Give me two, please.
examples.note: Simple base: even without naming the noun, 두 개 stands alone; note 둘 shortens to 두 right before the counter.

examples.en: There are three students in the classroom.
examples.note: Everyday order noun + number + counter: 명 is the counter for people, and 셋 becomes 세 before it (세 명, never 셋 명).

examples.en: I raise one puppy at home.
examples.note: 마리 is the animal counter, and 하나 contracts to 한 before it (한 마리, never 하나 마리).

examples.ko: 여기 삼겹살 2인분하고 소주 한 병 주세요.
examples.en: We'll have two servings of pork belly and one bottle of soju here.
examples.note: Real situation (ordering): 인분 'servings' rides the Sino number 2, while 병 'bottles' takes native 한 — a live reminder the two systems coexist in one breath.

commonMistakes: Using Sino numbers with counters: 이 개, 삼 명 instead of 두 개, 세 명. Counters demand native numbers; reserve 일·이·삼 for money, dates, and minutes (이천 원, 삼 분).
Forgetting that 1–4 shorten before the counter: 하나 개, 둘 명, 셋 마리 are wrong. They must contract to 한 개, 두 명, 세 마리. (Note: 스물 → 스무 also shortens, e.g. 스무 개.)
studyOrder: Pick the right counter: 개 things, 명 people, 마리 animals, 잔 cups, 병 bottles
Choose a native number
Change 1 to 4 to 한, 두, 세, 네 before the counter
Say it as noun + number + counter
beginnerExplanation: Korean cannot count things with a number alone; you need a counter word that matches the category, and you feed it a native number. Mnemonic: it's like English 'two SHEETS of paper, two CUPS of coffee' — the counter is the unit word. The everyday set is 개 for objects, 명 for people, 마리 for animals, 잔 for cups/glasses, 병 for bottles, giving 사과 두 개 (two apples) and 학생 세 명 (three students). The must-memorize rule is that native one-through-four shrink before a counter: 하나 둘 셋 넷 → 한 두 세 네, so 한 개, 두 명, 세 마리 (and 스물 → 스무). The classic pitfall is reaching for Sino numbers like 이 or 삼 — those belong to dates, money, and minutes, so counting people as 이 명 is wrong; you want 두 명. Word order is fixed: noun, then number, then counter.

title: Background or soft contrast
plainEnglish: It sets up background information or a gentle but before the next clause.
whenToUse: Use -는데 to lay down a situation first, then attach what you really want to say — a request, question, suggestion, surprise, or light contrast: 비가 오는데 우산 있어요? (it's raining — do you have an umbrella?), 주말인데 같이 영화 볼래요? (it's the weekend, so shall we see a movie?). The intent is to soften and connect: you set the scene so the next clause doesn't feel abrupt. It's the conversational glue Koreans lean on constantly, especially to open a polite request (실례지만, 길 좀 묻는데요…) or to flag a mild contrast without sounding confrontational.
attachmentRule: For verbs and 있다/없다 add -는데 to the stem (가는데, 먹는데). For adjectives add -은데 after a consonant and -ㄴ데 after a vowel (작은데, 큰데). Past tense uses -았/었는데 (갔는데).
contrastWith: Sharp contrast: -는데 vs -지만. -지만 is a blunt, pure 'but' that directly opposes two clauses (비싸지만 살게요 = it's expensive but I'll buy it). -는데 is softer and does double duty: it can contrast (맛있는데 비싸요) OR just set the stage with no opposition at all (지금 가는데 뭐 사 갈까? = I'm heading over — should I bring anything?), where -지만 would be impossible. Rule of thumb: if you could drop in 'and, by the way, so' as easily as 'but', use -는데.

examples.en: I'm hungry — what should we eat?
examples.note: Simple base: 배고프다 is an adjective, so it takes -ㄴ데 (배고픈데); here -는데 just sets up a suggestion, no contrast at all.

examples.ko: 이 식당 음식은 맛있는데 좀 비싸요.
examples.en: This restaurant's food is tasty, but it's a bit pricey.
examples.note: Everyday soft contrast: 있다-type 맛있다 takes -는데; 좀 'a bit' cushions the criticism, the very tone -는데 is built for.

examples.en: I'm studying Korean right now, and it's harder than I expected.
examples.note: Verb 공부하다 takes -는데 (공부하는데); this is pure background-then-comment, not contrast — the natural everyday feel of -는데.

examples.ko: 어제 그 카페에 갔는데 문을 닫았더라고요.
examples.en: I went to that cafe yesterday, but it turned out to be closed.
examples.note: Real situation with past tense: 갔는데 (가다 + 았 + 는데) gives background to a small story — note past always uses -았/었는데, never -은데.

commonMistakes: Using -은데 on a verb: 먹은데, 가은데 to mean 'eating, going'. Verbs (and 있다/없다) take -는데 → 먹는데, 가는데. -은데/-ㄴ데 is only for adjectives (작은데, 큰데).

Reaching for -는데 only when you mean a strong 'but': if the contrast is blunt and direct, use -지만 instead (비싸지만 살게요), and save -는데 for background or soft contrast. Conversely, don't force a hard 'but' reading onto 지금 공부하는데 너무 어려워요 — it mostly means 'I'm studying and wow, it's hard,' not 'I study BUT it's hard.'

practiceItems.prompt: it is the weekend, so (shall we watch a movie)

studyOrder: Decide if the word is a verb or an adjective
For verbs and 있다/없다 use -는데
For adjectives use -은데 or -ㄴ데
Add the reaction, request, or contrast in the next clause
beginnerExplanation: -는데 is the soft connector that paints the background first, then lets you add your real point — a reaction, a question, a request, or a gentle contrast. Mnemonic: think of it as 'setting the stage' — say the scene, comma, then the spotlight: 비가 오는데 우산이 없어요 (it's raining, comma, and I have no umbrella) or 주말인데 같이 영화 볼래요? (it's the weekend, comma, shall we see a movie?). Attachment depends on word type: verbs and 있다/없다 take -는데 (가는데, 먹는데, 맛있는데), while adjectives take -은데 after a consonant and -ㄴ데 after a vowel (작은데, 큰데). Past tense for everything is -았/었는데 (갔는데). The main pitfall is mixing these up and saying 먹은데 for a verb — verbs always use -는데. And remember this ending is far gentler than the blunt -지만 'but'; half the time it isn't 'but' at all, just 'and, so, by the way'.

title: Doing two things at once
plainEnglish: It links two actions that one person does at the same time.
whenToUse: Use -(으)면서 when ONE person genuinely overlaps two actions in the same stretch of time — multitasking: 음악을 들으면서 공부해요 (I study while listening to music), 밥을 먹으면서 텔레비전을 봐요 (I eat while watching TV). The intent is true simultaneity, both actions running together, so it fits 'while …-ing' perfectly. It also stretches to mean 'as / over the course of' for ongoing parallel states (한국에서 살면서 한국어를 배웠어요 = I learned Korean while living in Korea). Whenever you'd say English 'while doing X', and the same subject does both, this is your pattern.
attachmentRule: Attach -으면서 to a stem ending in a consonant (먹으면서, 읽으면서) and -면서 to a stem ending in a vowel (가면서, 보면서). The subject of both actions must be the same person.
contrastWith: Sharp contrast: -(으)면서 vs -고. -고 merely lists or sequences ('A and (then) B'): 밥을 먹고 텔레비전을 봐요 = I eat, then watch TV (one after the other). -(으)면서 forces the two to OVERLAP in time: 밥을 먹으면서 텔레비전을 봐요 = both at once. Swap test: if you can insert '그다음에 (after that)' it's -고; if both happen in the same moment, it's -(으)면서. Also note 면서 needs one shared subject; -고 can join different subjects.

examples.en: I go along singing.
examples.note: Simple base: vowel-final 하 takes plain -면서 (노래하면서); two actions, one body, same moment.

examples.en: I chat with a friend while drinking coffee.
examples.note: Everyday overlap: 마시다 ends in a vowel → -면서; the collocation 수다를 떨다 'chatter away' makes it sound like real speech.

examples.en: I cleaned my room while singing.
examples.note: 부르다 ends in a vowel → -면서 (부르면서); one person, two overlapping actions, the core meaning of the pattern.

examples.ko: 음악을 들으면서 운전하면 위험할 수도 있어요.
examples.en: It can be dangerous to drive while listening to music.
examples.note: Real situation + irregular: 듣다 is a ㄷ-irregular, so 듣 → 들 before -으면서 (들으면서), not 듣으면서.

commonMistakes: Using -(으)면서 with two different subjects: 제가 요리하면서 동생이 청소해요 to mean 'I cook while my sibling cleans' is wrong — both clauses must share ONE subject. For different doers use -는 동안 (제가 요리하는 동안 동생이 청소해요).
Dropping the linking 으 after a consonant: 먹면서, 읽면서. Consonant stems need -으면서 → 먹으면서, 읽으면서. (And don't forget irregulars: 듣다 → 들으면서.)
studyOrder: Check that one subject does both actions
Find the verb stem
Add -면서 after a vowel or -으면서 after a consonant
Put the simultaneous action in the second clause
beginnerExplanation: -(으)면서 joins two actions that one person performs at the very same time, exactly like English 'while …-ing'. Mnemonic: picture two hands busy at once — same body, same moment. The rule is one subject doing both: 음악을 들으면서 공부해요 (I study while listening to music) and 밥을 먹으면서 텔레비전을 봐요 (I watch TV while eating). Attachment follows the usual split: vowel-final stems take -면서 (가면서, 보면서) and consonant-final stems take -으면서 (먹으면서, 읽으면서) — and irregular 듣다 becomes 들으면서. Two pitfalls trip beginners up: don't use it when the clauses have different subjects (for that, use -는 동안 'during the time that'), and don't drop the linking 으 after a consonant, so it's 먹으면서, never 먹면서. Compare it with -고, which only lists actions ('A, then B') and does not force them to overlap.

title: Before doing something
plainEnglish: It says you do the main action before another action happens.
whenToUse: Use V-기 전에 to anchor one action 'before' another: name the LATER event right before 전에, and put what you do first in the main clause — 밥을 먹기 전에 손을 씻어요 (before eating, I wash my hands), 자기 전에 책을 읽어요 (before sleeping, I read). The intent is sequencing two events on a timeline, and it stays the same regardless of when the whole thing happens (past, present, future), because the tense lives in the final verb, not in 전에. Great for routines, instructions, and plans: 회의를 시작하기 전에 자료를 보내 주세요 (please send the materials before the meeting starts).
attachmentRule: Attach -기 전에 to any verb stem with no vowel or consonant change (먹기 전에, 가기 전에, 자기 전에). For before a noun, use Noun 전에 instead (식사 전에).
contrastWith: Sharp contrast: -기 전에 vs -(으)ㄴ 후에. They are mirror images: -기 전에 keeps the PLAIN stem and names what comes LATER (먹기 전에 = before eating), while -(으)ㄴ 후에 uses a past-style -은/-ㄴ form and names what comes EARLIER (먹은 후에 = after eating). One sequence, two viewpoints — choose by which action you frame as the reference point. Tip: 전에 = plain stem; 후에 = -은/-ㄴ stem. Mixing the stems (먹은 전에, 먹기 후에) is the giveaway error.

examples.en: I brush my teeth before bed.
examples.note: Simple base: 자다 → plain stem 자 + -기 전에 (자기 전에); no spelling change ever happens to the stem.

examples.ko: 밥을 먹기 전에 꼭 손을 씻어요.
examples.en: I always wash my hands before I eat.
examples.note: Everyday routine: 꼭 'without fail' is a natural partner here, and the later event 먹기 sits right before 전에.

examples.en: I drink plenty of water before exercising.
examples.note: 운동하다 → plain stem 운동하 + -기 전에; the later event (exercising) hugs 전에, the earlier one (drinking) is the main clause.

examples.ko: 한국에 오기 전에는 김치를 한 번도 안 먹어 봤어요.
examples.en: Before I came to Korea, I had never once eaten kimchi.
examples.note: Real situation: 오기 전에 can take 는 for contrast/emphasis (전에는), and the main clause carries the tense, not 전에.

commonMistakes: Conjugating the verb before -기 전에: 먹어기 전에, 갔기 전에. Always use the bare dictionary stem + -기 전에 → 먹기 전에, 가기 전에. Tense belongs to the final verb only, so 전에 itself never changes.
Using -기 전에 with a noun: 식사기 전에, 회의기 전에. With a noun you drop -기 and say Noun 전에 → 식사 전에, 회의 전에. -기 is only for verbs.

practiceItems.prompt: before going out (I turn off the light)

studyOrder: Find the action that happens later, the main verb
Take its plain dictionary stem
Add -기 전에 with no spelling change
Place the earlier event in the main clause
beginnerExplanation: V-기 전에 lets you say you do something before another action takes place, and it's wonderfully regular: just bolt -기 전에 onto the plain verb stem with zero changes. Mnemonic: 전 means 'before/front', so -기 전에 literally puts an action 'in front of' the timeline. Look at 밥을 먹기 전에 손을 씻어요 (I wash my hands before I eat) and 자기 전에 책을 읽어요 (I read before I sleep): the verb hugging 전에 is the LATER event, and the main clause tells what you do first. For nouns you switch to Noun 전에, as in 식사 전에 (before the meal), never 식사기 전에. The number-one pitfall is conjugating the verb — 먹어기 전에 is wrong; keep the bare stem 먹기, and let only the final verb carry the tense. Remember its mirror image -(으)ㄴ 후에 'after', and choose by which action you treat as the reference point: 전에 takes the plain stem, 후에 takes -은/-ㄴ.

title: After doing something
plainEnglish: It says you do the main action after another action is finished.
whenToUse: Use V-(으)ㄴ 후에 to place the main action 'after' another one has finished: name the EARLIER event before 후에, and put what follows in the main clause — 밥을 먹은 후에 커피를 마셔요 (after eating, I drink coffee), 수업이 끝난 후에 집에 가요 (after class ends, I go home). The intent is clean sequencing where step one fully wraps before step two. It suits routines, plans, and instructions, and the finished-first feeling is why it takes a past-style -은/-ㄴ form. Swap 후에 for 다음에 or 뒤에 freely; for events you don't fully complete first, prefer -고 나서.
attachmentRule: Add -은 후에 to a stem ending in a consonant (먹은 후에, 읽은 후에) and -ㄴ 후에 to a stem ending in a vowel (간 후에, 본 후에). For after a noun, use Noun 후에 (식사 후에). You can replace 후에 with 다음에 or 뒤에.
contrastWith: Sharp contrast: -(으)ㄴ 후에 vs -기 전에. Mirror images: 후에 uses the past-flavored -은/-ㄴ stem and names the EARLIER event (먹은 후에 = after eating), while 전에 uses the plain stem and names the LATER event (먹기 전에 = before eating). Also vs -고 나서: -고 나서 stresses 'and THEN, having finished' with a tighter cause/flow feel (손을 씻고 나서 먹어요), whereas -(으)ㄴ 후에 simply marks the time order 'after'. Stem test: 후에 → -은/-ㄴ; 전에 → plain -기.

examples.en: I shower after working out.
examples.note: Simple base: 운동하다 → vowel-ending 하 takes -ㄴ 후에 (운동한 후에), the same -ㄴ you see on past modifiers.

examples.en: I eat after washing my hands.
examples.note: Everyday consonant stem: 씻다 ends in a consonant → -은 후에 (씻은 후에); the earlier action sits right before 후에.

examples.en: I drink coffee after I eat.
examples.note: 먹다 ends in a consonant → -은 후에 (먹은 후에); the earlier action (eating) sits before 후에, the later one (coffee) follows.

examples.ko: 수업이 끝난 후에 같이 저녁 먹을래요?
examples.en: After class ends, do you want to grab dinner together?
examples.note: Real situation: 후에 swaps cleanly to 다음에/뒤에 (끝난 다음에), and the main clause can be a present-tense invitation.

commonMistakes: Reusing the plain -기 stem from the 'before' pattern: 먹기 후에, 가기 후에. 'After' needs the -은/-ㄴ form → 먹은 후에, 간 후에. If you wrote -기, you built 'before', not 'after'.
Ignoring the consonant/vowel split: 가은 후에, 보은 후에. Vowel stems take -ㄴ 후에 (간 후에, 본 후에); only consonant stems take -은 후에 (먹은 후에).
studyOrder: Find the action that happens first
Add -은 후에 after a consonant or -ㄴ 후에 after a vowel
Put the later action in the main clause
Swap 후에 for 다음에 or 뒤에 if you like
beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 후에 expresses that you do the main action after another one is finished, and it's the exact opposite of -기 전에. Mnemonic: 후 means 'after/behind', so this pattern sits an action 'behind' you on the timeline — done and dusted. Unlike 'before', the 'after' pattern uses the -은/-ㄴ ending (the same shape as a past modifier): consonant stems take -은 후에 (먹은 후에, 읽은 후에) and vowel stems take -ㄴ 후에 (간 후에, 본 후에). So 밥을 먹은 후에 커피를 마셔요 means I drink coffee after eating, and 수업이 끝난 후에 집에 가요 means I go home after class ends; the verb before 후에 is the EARLIER event. For nouns use Noun 후에, like 식사 후에, and feel free to swap 후에 for 다음에 or 뒤에. The main pitfall is borrowing the plain -기 stem from 'before' — for 'after' you must say 먹은 후에, not 먹기 후에. If you want a tighter 'and then' flavor, -고 나서 (먹고 나서) is the neighbor to know.

title: Every or each
plainEnglish: It attaches to a noun to mean every or each one.
whenToUse: Use N마다 to mean 'every' over a repeating time or 'each' across members of a set. With time words it gives regular repetition: 주말마다 운동해요 (I exercise every weekend), 아침마다 커피를 마셔요 (every morning). With people or things it distributes one-by-one: 사람마다 생각이 달라요 (each person thinks differently), 가게마다 가격이 달라요 (prices differ from shop to shop). The intent is 'without exception, for every single one', so reach for it whenever English would say 'every X' or 'each X' and you want it to ride directly on the noun. It's everyday and neutral in register.
attachmentRule: Attach 마다 directly to the noun after both vowels and consonants with no change (아침마다, 주말마다, 사람마다). With time words it means every; with people or things it means each.
contrastWith: Sharp contrast: 마다 vs the prefix 매-. 마다 is a particle that clips onto almost any noun, including ones 매- can't touch (사람마다, 가게마다, 나라마다). 매- is a fixed Sino prefix that only forms set vocabulary on time units — 매일 (every day), 매주, 매달, 매년 — and you can't say 매주말 or 매사람. So 매일 ≈ 날마다, but for 'each person' only 사람마다 works. Don't double them up (매일마다 is redundant).

examples.en: I exercise every day.
examples.note: Simple base: 날마다 ≈ 매일; with a time word 마다 reads as plain 'every', riding straight on the noun.

examples.en: The bus comes every ten minutes.
examples.note: Everyday interval: 마다 attaches to a number+counter (십 분마다) to mean 'at every … interval' — a super common scheduling use.

examples.en: Each person likes different food.
examples.note: The signature 'each' use: 사람마다 distributes over every individual, so it cannot become 매사람 — only 마다 works on 사람.

examples.en: The way people greet differs from country to country.
examples.note: Real situation: with a non-time noun 마다 means 'each', and it pairs naturally with 다르다 'differ' (…마다 … 달라요).

commonMistakes: Stacking a particle after 마다: 주말마다에, 아침마다에. 마다 already works as the adverbial 'every', so no 에 follows → 주말마다 운동해요. (Don't add 에 the way you would to a bare time noun like 주말에.)
Confusing 마다 with 매- and over-forming words: 매주말, 매사람 don't exist, and 매일마다 is redundant. Use 매- only on its fixed set (매일/매주/매달/매년); for everything else, attach 마다 (주말마다, 사람마다).
studyOrder: Pick the noun you want to repeat or distribute
Attach 마다 directly with no spelling change
Read it as every for time words
Read it as each for people or things
beginnerExplanation: N마다 attaches to a noun and means 'every' or 'each', covering both repeated times and every member of a group. Mnemonic: think 'one by one, no exceptions' — 마다 sweeps through every single item. With time words it lands on 'every': 주말마다 운동해요 (every weekend), 아침마다 커피를 마셔요 (every morning), and it even rides intervals like 십 분마다 (every ten minutes). With people or things it shades to 'each': 사람마다 생각이 달라요 (each person thinks differently). Attachment couldn't be simpler — 마다 glues straight onto the noun after both vowels and consonants with no change. Two pitfalls: don't pile another particle on top (avoid 주말마다에, since 마다 already does the adverb's job), and don't confuse it with the prefix 매-, which only lives on fixed words like 매일 or 매주. 마다 attaches freely to almost any noun, so for 'each person' it's 사람마다 — there is no 매사람.
